content:
Facts: Pretermitted children obtained final judgments establishing sale simulation concealing father's donation to brother (who resold half to another brother) and reducing donation for legitimate portion infringement (1/14 each); sued for heir status declaration, collation, division, restitution with demolition of erected buildings, or equivalent monetary compensation; third brother joined claiming same relief; defendants objected to limitation and claims' merits.
Legal Framework: Articles 555, 560, 563, 713 et seq., 737 Italian Civil Code (reduction effects; reintegration modalities; third-party purchaser liability; division rules; collation); established case law on reduction-division relationship (Cass. 25441/2017, 16635/2013, 1971/1964, 4005/1974, 3177/1971, 5042/2011).
Interpretive Issues: Whether totally pretermitted heir acquires heir status before or after successful reduction action finality; admissibility of combining reduction with division for comunio incidens re-establishment; collation availability when estate exhausted by donations/bequests with no relictum; distinction between reduction action and consequential reintegration claims (in kind versus equivalent); personal versus universal effects of reduction judgment for non-acting co-heirs; third-party purchaser liability scope when legitimate heir waives in-kind restitution choosing monetary equivalent; burden regarding donee asset enforcement before pursuing purchaser; limitation period applicability when restitution claim abandoned.
Principles Applied: Totally pretermitted legitimate heir acquires heir status only after successful reduction action becomes final; pretermitation occurs even in intestate succession when deceased disposed assets via lifetime donations. Inheritance acquisition through successful reduction per Art. 555 produces effects limited to independently acting legitimate heirs for their reserved portion fraction. Collation presupposes estate joint ownership and divisible assets; unfounded when assets exhausted by donations/bequests leaving no relictum to divide except reduction outcome. Collation per Art. 737 targets other donated assets against liable parties, not residual assets or donations already reduced. Reduction of specific-asset gifts (legacies/donations) establishes sui generis joint ownership between donee/legatee and successful legitimate heir under Art. 560 special rules. Reintegration permitted in specific form or by equivalent; donee/legatee may retain asset compensating legitimate heir in cash; legitimate heir may renounce in-kind portion requesting monetary value. Combination of reduction with division admissible for re-establishing comunio incidens between legitimate heirs for limited reinstatement purpose through partial detachment of excessively assigned assets. Reduction and restitution constitute different actions with distinct legal effects; dispositive principle rigour requires separate assertion. Prior judgment declaring donation ineffective within legitimate portion limits without ruling restitution modalities permits subsequent implementation claims; no res judicata formed. Waiver of in-kind reintegration request maintaining only equivalent-value claim eliminates divisibility assessment and donee retention objection issues. Reduction judgment's constitutive (non-declaratory) nature diversifies reduction claim from consequential reintegration claim despite connection. Personal reduction judgment effects not communicated to non-acting heirs; third-party heir cannot benefit from siblings' successful reduction absent own independent action. Third-party purchaser liability per Art. 563 requires legitimate heir prove unsuccessful donee asset enforcement attempt; burden includes proving sale price recovery attempt futility or total insolvency. Monetary adjustment constitutes value debt requiring revaluation to decision-time asset value plus compensatory interest on revalued amount from claim date. Twenty-year limitation under Art. 563 absorbed when actual restitution claim against purchaser abandoned. Tacit waiver occurs through unambiguous conclusion reformulation omitting previously asserted claims.
